content.thinking:
I need to carefully plan the dwarf's design before writing: a short, stocky 1.25m figure with a big head, wide shoulders, thick arms, short legs, huge boots, a braided beard, helmet, and blunderbuss, built around a skeleton rooted at the hips with a spine chain running up through chest and neck.

I'm working out exact joint positions in meters—hips, knees, ankles, shoulders, neck, and head center—aiming for a total height around 1.3m including the helmet, then mapping these into joint and chain calls while being careful that the number of names matches the number of spans in each chain.

Now I'm sketching the neck, head, and jaw joints, specifying their positions and aim directions so the head sits forward and slightly up, and planning the jaw as a small forward-angled bone off the head joint.

For the torso, I'm setting up a loft shape following the spine chain, defining width and depth stations at each vertical height so the body tapers and bulges naturally — narrower at the waist, wider through the chest, with the belly pushed slightly forward.

I'm thinking through how spans are weighted along the chain so the first segment before spine1 still gets proper coverage, just using the spine bone reference alone to simplify things.

Now I'm setting up the leg positions, mirroring left and right using a sign multiplier for the x-offset.

With 3 points giving 2 spans plus the tip joint, I'll parent the leg to the hips and sweep the chain with tapering radii from thick thigh to narrower ankle, painted as pants. For the boot, I'm attaching a chunky box geometry rigidly to the ankle bone, positioned to cover the foot.

Shaping the capsule foot and shaft...

I'll have boots sweep over the lower shin with a shaft capsule between ankle and knee, plus a small knee pad sphere for detail. For the arms, I'm setting up shoulder joints and planning the chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist to hand tip.

For the pose, I'm going with the classic WoW rifleman stance — dwarf standing in a neutral A-pose with the blunderbuss held in the right hand, muzzle pointing up and butt resting on the floor like a walking staff, with the butt touching ground at x=-0.36.

Working out the right arm joint positions: shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates that bring the hand to grip the stock around waist height, with the gun oriented vertically so the butt meets the floor and the muzzle flares upward. The left arm stays relaxed in A-pose with an open hand resting near the hip.

The reach of 0.47 against a limb length of 0.5 needs only a slight elbow bend, so that's fine. Now for the grip, I need the fist to wrap around the gun's axis, so I'm aligning the hand center close to the gun's centerline near [-0.37, 0.52, 0.13] so the fingers appear to clasp it naturally.

I'm building the fist as a box roughly covering the grip, hiding the thin gun barrel inside, then adding four short capsules stacked along y to represent knuckles wrapping the front, plus a vertical thumb capsule to complete the grip illusion.

Now working out the left arm: shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints positioned with the hand resting near the hip in a loose fist, computing upper and forearm segment lengths to match the natural A-pose stance.

I'm settling on an open hand hanging naturally with slightly spread fingers for the rig, then planning the finger structure—four fingers with two joints each plus a thumb on the left hand, while keeping the right hand as a closed fist, staying within the joint budget.

Right hand stays rigid as a fist holding the gun to keep things simple, while I build out the left hand's finger chains properly. For the arm chain itself, I'm naming the shoulder-elbow-wrist joints per side, setting the wrist as the tip, tagging the role as "arm," and parenting it to the chest joint in the spine.

For the arm's visual sweep, I'm tapering the radius from upper arm to forearm with a bracer bulge, using color bands to split sleeve fabric from bare skin, and layering a separate leather bracer sweep over part of the forearm. Now I'm starting on the pauldron shoulder armor piece.

Still writing shoulder geometry...

Then I move to planning the head: setting a head center point and joint position, keeping the structure simple with basic constants for now.

For the facial details I'm thinking big dwarf-style features — oversized nose, bushy brows, a beard covering the lower face — with a ruddy skin tone, going for a hand-painted gradient look rather than a toon/cel style to match the Blizzard-esque aesthetic.

I'm defining a shading helper that blends a darker cool tone with a warmer highlight based on surface normal, plus optional subtle noise for mottled texture variation.

Now I'm building the skull geometry: a scaled sphere for the head, cheek bumps, a bulbous nose with nostrils, and a brow ridge with bushy eyebrow capsules.

Working out eye placement next, I'm computing where the eye sockets sit on the curved head surface so I can embed small white sphere "eyes" with darker iris/pupil spheres at roughly the right depth.

Now I'm positioning the nose protruding from the face center with a reddish tint for the dwarf's bulbous look, then starting to sketch out a beard mass sweeping from the chin down to the chest using a curved path.

For the beard radius, I'm making it wide at the cheeks and tapering narrower toward the belly, with depth going forward rather than flat against the face. I'll paint it ginger-orange with fine strand-like grain running along the length, and attach the whole mass rigidly to the head bone so it moves naturally with the head.

Next I'm sweeping out a curling mustache from under the nose using a short catmull curve on each side, radius tapering down near the tips, colored to match the beard. Then I want to add two long braids hanging off the sides of the beard.

Each braid follows a curved path from the chin down to around belly height, with a sequence of small spheres strung along it to suggest braided segments -- I'll loop through points along the path, alternating scale and maybe color between adjacent spheres rather than relying on the built-in along-callback.

For the jaw, I'm separating it from the main head: a small chin-shaped blob attached to a jaw bone so it can move independently, mostly concealed under the beard mesh, and skipping visible teeth since they'd be hidden anyway.

Now I'm adding dwarf ears -- slightly pointed spheres positioned on either side of the head with tiny gold ring torus earrings attached -- and starting on the helmet, building a lathed dome profile for an iron bowl shape with a brass trim detail at the base.

I'm checking the helmet's placement against the head geometry, raising its base so the brim sits above the eyes rather than overlapping them, and verifying the resulting total height stays reasonably proportioned for a dwarf figure, considering scaling down slightly if it ends up too tall.

Now I'm sketching curved horns sweeping up from the sides of the helmet using a swept path with tapering radius toward the tips, positioned so they rise above the helmet crown.

Settling on an overall figure height around 1.38, close enough to the target range. For the helmet, I'm adding a brass torus band around the brim, a ring of rivet spheres, and a front-to-back crest ridge arcing over the dome using a curved sweep.

Working out the dome's lathe profile and matching crest ridge coordinates...

I'm deciding to skip the nose guard since it would conflict with the nose geometry, and also skipping earflaps to keep the helmet simpler. Now I'm moving to torso clothing, planning a dwarven look with a tunic and breastplate — royal blue tunic and brown leather pants as the base palette.

For the breastplate, I'm shaping a flattened sphere as a steel chest plate with a small gold octahedron gem as a central emblem instead of any logo, and considering skipping extra ridge details on the rim to keep it simple.

Next I'm working out the belt as a closed catmull-rom curve swept around the torso's waist at the right radius, forming a flat horizontal band tube using the proper binormal orientation for a sweep around a horizontal loop.

I'll use a flattened cylinder scaled on the z-axis to approximate an elliptical belt matching the torso's dimensions at that height, attached near spine1, then add a gold buckle box on top.

Now I'm planning pouches on the hips and a bandolier strap draped diagonally across the chest, routing its path above the breastplate surface so it doesn't clip through the armor.

Still placing cartridges...

Simplifying the approach, I'll use small brass cylinders to represent cartridges, positioning each centered on the strap's path and embedding part of their height so they sit flush on the surface.

Now I'm planning a powder horn hanging from the left hip belt via a cord, using a curved path that sweeps down and out from the hip with a tapering radius to resemble a horn shape.

On the gun side I'll add a shot pouch box with a flap near the right hip, keeping it clear of the arm. For the back, I'm adding a backpack with a bedroll strapped across the top and a cooking pot, positioned so it's visible since the scene is lit mostly from the front. Now considering whether to add a cape or tabard over the shoulders.

For the front I'll hang a short tabard from the belt using an extruded cloth shape with a tapered hem, colored dark red with gold trim, moving with the hip bone. I'm thinking about decorating it with a simple heraldic emblem via a flat plane texture — avoiding anything derivative, so leaning toward an original design like a golden sun rather than anything evoking existing game iconography.

Adjusting the tabard to z 0.14 so it sits closer to the thighs, then adding gold trim along the outline edges using a thin swept rod rather than tilting the whole piece. For the skirt I'll stick with the loft approach, and now I need to work out the neck sweep connecting the torso to the head.

For the blunderbuss, the hero prop, I'm positioning it vertically near x=-0.37 with the muzzle flaring upward around y=1.05-1.08, resting butt-down on the floor rather than held at ready — a grounded, standing pose feels more fitting. I'm working out the curved stock geometry from butt to wrist to barrel flare.

Defining stock segments...

Adding the lock plate and receiver as a small brass box with a hammer and trigger guard torus, trying to figure out which side should face forward for display since the gun points vertically upward.

Positioning the trigger as a small box and placing the hammer at the back of the lock for visibility, with a flat engraved lockplate on the side face. For the barrel, I'm planning a tapered sweep that flares from the breech outward, like a classic blunderbuss bell shape.

Now I'm working out a hollow lathe-shell profile for the flared mouth, defining outer and inner contour points that loop up, across the rim, and back down to close the polygon.

Now I'm adding the steel octagonal barrel with brass collar rings at intervals, a gold mouth collar, and a thin ramrod running underneath the barrel.

I'm also sketching a leather sling strap curving from barrel to stock with swivels, then positioning the hand grip around the wrist/stock area, working out where the fist and wrist should sit relative to the gun's axis.

Checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance against the arm segment lengths to make sure the pose is reachable without overextending, then setting up the mirrored left arm similarly.

Now I realize the hand/fist position overlaps with where the gun's lock mechanism sits, so I need to rework the vertical layout: shifting the stock lower and the lock/barrel higher so the gripping hand doesn't collide with the lock geometry.

I'll rig the gun parts to the right wrist bone so it moves naturally with the hand, with the butt resting on the floor in rest pose. For the left hand, I'm building palm geometry and four finger chains (base/mid/tip joints) hanging down from the wrist with slight spread and forward curl, scaled up a bit for oversized hands.

Working out finger placement...

For the arm chain, the tip joint is the wrist, giving three joint names spanning two bone segments plus the tip. For the right hand gripping the gun, I need to figure out how the fingers curl around the stock from the palm side while keeping everything rigid.

Working out finger geometry...

I'll place the thumb capsule crossing over the fingers, and decide to give both hands bare skin with metal bracers instead of gloves for simplicity. Now I'm setting up a paint helper utility with functions for mixing, noise, smoothstep, and mottling to generate the skin tones and surface details without blowing past the flat color budget.

Writing paint helpers...

Finishing the lit() function...

Now I'm checking the noise call signature with position, size, and seed, and thinking through how to layer this for beard and skin paints—applying grain texture to the beard and considering mottle for skin blush.

Steel, gold, leather, wood stock, and cloth each need their own paint treatment—mostly variations of mottle and grain with different scale and contrast parameters. I'm estimating texel density across the total painted surface area to make sure resolution holds up at the chosen atlas size.

I'm aiming to keep the part count manageable, around 250, well under any budget limit, and reasoning through which colors need to be flat strings (eyes, small accents) versus paint-driven materials, since only flat colors count toward distinct color budgets. Now I'm setting up a small helper function to shorten part-creation calls, and working out the right type signature for color inputs—deciding whether to type it as string or Paint to match the Fill type expected by the system.

I'm pulling in the Fill type from the context module since it's properly exported, and planning out geometry helper functions for spheres, boxes, and cylinders with configurable segment counts, relying on low segment counts to give that chunky, hand-painted faceted look without extra flat-shading flags. I'm also tracking which imports I'll actually need (builder, Fill, limb/IK helpers, path utilities, paint effects like mix, noise, smoothstep, grain, mottle, stripes, and possibly a glow effect for gems) so I don't end up with unused import errors.

Now I'm working out how to add beard texture using surface-scattered hair cards, flowing downward and tapering, with their own ginger/orange gradient coloring rather than relying on a generic tint.

I'm also planning the beard geometry itself as layered sweeps—a main sweep plus side locks curving from the cheeks down and inward, tapering in radius, alongside keeping the SVG assets limited to tabard emblem and beard tuft shapes.

Adding forked chin braids that hang in front of the belly, extending slightly past the belt line with brass ring ties at the ends, while the main beard mass hangs higher up.

I'm checking that the chest plate's z-extent sits just behind the beard's front profile so the beard visibly overlaps and covers the plate near the chin, then working out a radius function for the beard sweep to make sure it hugs the lower face near the cheeks without clipping into the skull surface.

Now I'm plotting the beard path points down the chin with decreasing widths and radii, making sure the beard's front radius exceeds the face surface at each height so it visibly covers the cheeks and chin, then moving to work out sideburn spheres connecting ear to chin.

Then I'm shaping the mustache as a swept path curving outward and down from under the nose, tapering its radius toward the ends, and adding a small pink lower lip sphere peeking out beneath it since the mouth itself will mostly be hidden by the beard.

Now I'm working on bushy eyebrows as tapered sweeps positioned above each eye, matching the ginger beard color, and checking that their vertical placement and radius give a good overhang above the eye sockets based on the head's surface curvature at that position.

Wait, the helmet brim sits at y1.19 with radius .158, which could cut right through the brow region—forehead gets hidden by the helmet, and the brows at y1.2+ might actually land inside the helmet bowl rather than protruding past it. I need to check whether the brow's outward position at z.18 clears the helmet's front surface or gets swallowed by it.

So I'm recalculating: brim depth comes to z.178, meaning brows poke through just slightly, but it risks looking like the helmet rests directly on the brows. Let me shift the whole head center down to y1.13, adjust eyes to 1.16, brows to 1.185, nose to 1.13, mustache to 1.095, and move the helmet base up to 1.2 so the brim sits right at the top of the brow—keeping the helmet covering the skull from 1.2 to 1.27 with a small air gap in the bowl, topping out around 1.385. Now I'm working through the surface normalization math to confirm the brow and eye positions land correctly relative to this adjusted head geometry.

I'm placing the beard to start around y1.10, with mustache around 1.09-1.1 and the main beard mass at y1.10, confirming the head bottom and chin region line up. I'm defining joint positions for the neck and jaw bones, with a lower jaw sphere hidden by the beard, and setting up a neck capsule that stays hidden under the collar. I'm also sketching the torso top dimensions and starting to add a steel gorget ring around the neck area.

Still defining leg chains...

Still adding boot details...

Still shaping boot geometry... adding a sole box, maybe a brass toe cap sphere, and a shaft capsule from ankle to shin with a flared cuff torus at the top.

I'm angling the cuff torus to match the shin's slight forward tilt rather than keeping it perfectly horizontal, and reusing the same leg function for both sides. For the torso, I'm thinking blue tunic with leather straps and a steel breastplate, maybe adding a chainmail skirt too.

Rather than overlapping fauld plates, I'll go simpler with a tabard and belt plus a large buckle. I'm sketching out the spine joint hierarchy with points from waist up to chest, naming them spine1, spine2, and chest, so pauldrons and other upper-body parts can attach as children of the chest joint. Then I'm planning a leather backpack box with a bedroll attached at the back.

Adding bedroll cylinder, leather strap bands, buckles, and a small tin cup to the pack, while skipping a hanging pot. I'm also considering simplified shoulder strap paths draping from the pack to the belt front.

For the eyes, I'm placing a sclera sphere, a colored iris, a dark pupil, and a tiny white specular highlight, all offset slightly in z to layer properly despite some geometry overlap.

For eyelids, I'm using a flattened skin-colored sphere scaled down in height as an upper lid cap, positioned to give a heavy-lidded, angry expression. Skipping blush since mottling handles that visually.

For ears, I'm scaling a small sphere for the base shape and adding an outward-pointing cone tip to suggest a pointed ear silhouette.

Now I'm adding a gold earring torus and planning the arms: exaggerated oversized fists, with sleeve bands that transition from a blue rolled sleeve at the shoulder to bare skin-colored forearm past the elbow, using a torus to represent the rolled cuff at the elbow joint position.

I'm also working out a bracer sweep over the forearm with a slightly tapered radius function to sit just above the natural forearm taper.

Finalizing the bracer taper function, then adding steel paint with gold trim rings and rivets. I'm moving to the hand geometry, defining the wrist joint, palm box, and finger base positions for both arms.

Setting up finger chains with proper joint naming and sweep radii, then addressing left wrist placement coordinates to line up with the target pose.

Still positioning hand geometry and palm shape, then working out the right hand's wrist and grip placement relative to the gun stock.

Still modeling finger geometry...

For the palm I'm bridging it with a scaled sphere, then sweeping the thumb as a curved capsule chain with its own radius, and pulling the wrist joint position from the arm's joint array to anchor the gun grip.

Now I'm moving to shoulder armor, building domed pauldrons with an open-bottom sphere geometry, scaling it to close the shape and adding a torus rim for a finished edge, then layering a second smaller dome beneath with its own tilt and positioning.

I'll reuse that same dir vector for the dome's orientation, then build the pauldron's rim torus, a scaled dome, pole spikes, and a ring of small gold studs positioned around the rim.

Writing ringPts helper...

Now I'm placing pauldron rim studs along that ring at radius 0.125 with small sphere bumps, and deciding on a gold lit metal color for the paint. I'm starting to lay out the gun parts next, planning the pole position and bone weighting.

Still writing gun geometry...

Checking the tapered stock width matches at y=.2, then placing the lock box with steel side plates, and sketching a hammer mechanism as a tapered steel curve from the lock up to the pan.

Now I'm adding the trigger guard as a gold torus ring, a small cone trigger, then building the tapered steel barrel as a swept octagonal profile, and spacing gold torus bands along its length.

Working on the breech transition and bell mouth flare now, lathing a tapered profile with outer and inner curves so the muzzle widens smoothly from the barrel's radius while keeping everything aligned at the correct heights.

I'm adding a gold rim torus and a dark recessed disc for the bore interior, then positioning the ramrod alongside the barrel—checking its radius against the barrel so it doesn't overlap, and nudging its z-offset outward so it floats properly beside the barrel rather than clipping through it.

I'll add a hanging red cord ribbon tied at the band, swept with a few catmull points down to a small gold tassel for detail. Skipping the sight blade, keeping legs in a plain standing rest pose, with the gun rigid against the wrist. Now I'm moving on to the pack and pouches.

For hip gear, I'm placing a leather shot pouch on the right hip with a buckled flap and gold button, parented to the hips bone since it governs the pelvis and legs, plus a powder horn on the left; skipping the dagger sheath and hatchet to keep part count reasonable. Now I'm sketching out the SVG textures for the emblem and beard tuft details.

Writing SVG code...

Then for the tabard, I'm planning a red cloth color with lit paint rendering, using a plane geometry with transparent cut corners and white tint passed through for textured parts so the underlying colors show properly.

Now I'm positioning the tabard mesh as an extruded shape along the body's front, defining its outline points to taper from the shoulders down to a point at the bottom, and figuring out the emblem plane placement slightly in front of the tabard surface, aligned with the model's coordinate axes.

I'm working through where the tabard should hang relative to the belt, adjusting its vertical offset and depth so it sits naturally in front of the torso without clipping into the belt cylinder, and sketching loft stations at different heights with varying widths and z-offsets to shape the torso silhouette.

Now I'm sizing the belt cylinder so it sits just outside the torso surface at that height, solving for the radius and z-scale so the belt protrudes slightly beyond the chest/belly contour instead of sinking under it.

Next I'm positioning the tabard and buckle just in front of the belt, then thinking about how the tabard should hang between the thighs below the belt line without rotation params available for the extrude, trying to figure out if it needs to stand off or tilt.

I'm computing the extrude direction vectors so the tabard tilts slightly forward (about 14°), cross-checking the axis math for the thickness direction, and then positioning the emblem plane at the top of the tabard angled along that same tilted downward vector.

Now I'm ready to assemble the full component, adding export metadata (name, description, style, commit hash), and being careful about TypeScript strictness around unused variables and possibly-undefined array indices from limb calculations—planning to use safe destructuring with non-null assertions where needed.

Writing imports and setup...

I'm figuring out where to apply glow for gems on the buckle and eyes, and considering whether stripes would work for a bedroll pattern using a red-and-tan color scheme along one axis.

Now I'm defining color constants and the main build function for the dwarf rifleman model, setting up helper functions for spheres, boxes, and cylinders to construct the geometry.

Building the skeleton hierarchy now...

Writing leg chain code...

Working out the boot shaft placement, identifying which joint indices correspond to knee and ankle, and figuring out the capsule geometry so the boot rigidly follows the knee bone while the ankle moves independently.

Now adding the cuff torus at the shin top, a knee guard sphere flattened and offset outward with a gold rivet accent, and considering a leather thigh strap as a decorative element.

For the foot, I'm building an ankle capsule joint bound to the leg skeleton, a heel block, a steel toe cap sphere squashed into shape, and a flat sole box sized to peek out from the sides of the boot capsule.

Adding straps with a buckle around the boot cuff, then confirming the ankle joint sits hidden at the proper height before moving into torso and arm details. Now I'm setting up the arm chains mirrored left and right, defining shoulder and wrist points to build the limb joints off the chest.

Checking shoulder placement against the torso's width so the joint sits just outside the edge under the pauldron, then working out the sweep radii tapering down the arm with a rolled sleeve band ending partway to the elbow, followed by a cuff torus marking where the sleeve stops.

The shoulder joint feeds the pauldron placement, and the wrist joint anchors the finger chain parenting. I'm planning to structure arm construction as a reusable function returning the chain and points so both arms can be built from one call, with the right wrist stored separately for attaching the gun.

Now I'm working out the beard: coloring with a grained lit paint for texture, then designing a braid with a catmull path, a thin darker core sweep, and alternating beads offset in a zigzag pattern along the braid length.

I realize the braid end would float in open air in front of the belly if left straight, so I'm curving the path back toward the body near the bottom, letting it rest against the belt area instead with just a slight gap from the belly surface.

Checking clearance against the chest plate, I'm computing the ellipsoid's front z-extent at various heights to confirm the braid stays just outside the plate surface rather than clipping into it, and verifying the plate itself sits correctly against the torso with its back half tucked inside.

I'm sketching a vertical gold ridge rod running along the plate's centerline using a curved path, then planning a ring of gold rivets spaced around the plate's rim at 14 evenly distributed angles.

For the centerpiece, I'm placing a glowing red gem (an icosahedron for the ruby) inside a gold torus setting at the plate's center, computing the rim position so the rivets sit flush with the curved surface.

Then I'm shifting to the torso's paint color, adding a gorget collar made from a steel torus with a gold rim tube that hugs the neck, and finally working out the belt buckle geometry—a gold outer box with a darker inset box set slightly forward in z.

Now I'm adding the backpack details: a leather flap, buckles, and a bedroll cylinder positioned on top with painted stripe bands across it.

I'm adding small strap cylinders at the pack sides, a steel tin cup with a handle near the hip, and skipping extra gear like an axe or spare lantern. Then I'm verifying the helmet geometry aligns properly over the skull's top, checking that the interior radius at the relevant height matches the head shape.

I'm defining the helmet's lathe profile with points moving from the base brim up to the rounded crown, then adding a brim band and gold torus trim at the brim line while skipping a nasal guard.

Still working out rivets, cheek guards, and horns...

I'm deciding to skip the plume and keep a simple crest rod instead, then adding ginger sideburns and beard hair under the helmet with a ruddy skin tone. I'm scattering tuft cards across the beard surface using a filtered hit pattern to control density and placement.

Writing tapered tuft SVG...

I'm placing the gun and checking it against the right pauldron and arm geometry for overlap, comparing the bell mouth radius and position against the pauldron's dome extent in x and z to spot potential collisions.

Trying to resolve the conflict by nudging the gun forward and outward and shortening the barrel, but recalculating shows the bell mouth still overlaps the pauldron's outer tilted rim at that height, so I'll need to adjust positioning further.

The elbow bend is minimal, making the arm nearly straight — a bit stiff but acceptable; I'll adjust the wrist target to [-0.42, 0.5, 0.15] so the palm sits near the stock rear at z .155, scaling the palm sphere accordingly.

I'm checking the stock-to-foot alignment and ribbon details look fine, so now I'm ready to write the final code: setting up the `put(g, c, bone, at, o)` helper with proper `Joint` typing imported from the skeleton module, using standard for-of loops for symmetry, adding a beads function, and defining the skin and other color palettes as lit paints at the top of the file.

Still writing palette definitions...

Defining more color palettes...

I'm double-checking the color inputs and part parameters for runtime correctness, verifying things like polyline point counts matching chain names and limb bend arrays before finalizing the file.

Now checking the sweep and drape functions for the straps and decorative elements, confirming the path signatures and nested surface targets work correctly with the stick placement along the draped path.

I'm working out cartridge geometry for the bandolier, orienting cylinders along the belt's tangent direction and coloring them brass/gold, then plotting the drape path points across the torso from right shoulder down to left hip, following the plate's contour.

Now I'm checking those drape points against the torso's surface geometry to make sure the strap falls naturally over the shoulder and pauldron. Then I'm setting up the tabard extrusion with its outline points, extruding along normalized x/y directions with red coloring and thickness, attached to the hip bone.

Adding trim sweep geometry...

I'll skip tiny fringe tassels for now and move on to finishing the pauldrons, confirming shoulder naming conventions and joint attachments before writing out the full build function with randomized seeding.

Defining the torso loft...

Head looks fine. Now I'm adding head detail parts, placing a sphere for the skull and small spheres for the cheeks with slight scale adjustments for roundness.

Still writing facial feature code...

I'm adding the chin, lips, and eyes attached to the jaw and head bones, then working through a beard sweep using a radius function and double-checking that TypeScript will correctly infer the tuple return type for the array literal.

Since I'm not fully confident in contextual typing here, I'll explicitly annotate the radius function's return type as a two-element number tuple to avoid inference errors, then move on to chin tufts, cheek locks, and the mustache. I'm also setting up horn bands with gold coloring and finalizing the build by returning the root bone structure, while planning a loop-based approach to construct left and right pauldrons and arms symmetrically by mirroring a sign value.

I'm working out the pauldron geometry — positioning the dome layers, gold trim rings, stud rings, and spike cones using angle and offset calculations relative to each shoulder joint, then moving on to straps, hands, and gun placement using the right arm's joint reference, before writing the finger construction logic for the left hand.

Now I'm figuring out the finger curve sweeps for both hands, using Catmull-Rom splines and bone attachments to position each joint's skin-colored tubes, and double-checking wrist and palm coordinates before finalizing the file with correct nesting and the glow import path.

I'm placing the powder horn asset and adjusting its path coordinates so it doesn't overlap the left hand's wrist position, shifting the horn's x-values inward to keep proper spacing from the palm.
